Nitokra spinipes is a brackish-water harpacticoid copepod whose early life history has been characterized under controlled laboratory conditions. Newly hatched nauplii emerge from subitaneous eggs after an incubation period of 3.17 days  when reared at 22 °C [T = 22 °C], a developmental duration that aligns closely with values reported for other harpacticoids of similar body size. The isometric length at hatch, measured immediately after egg fertilisation, is 0.0078 centimeters , representing a minute but critical starting point for the subsequent rapid pre-pubertal accelerating stage. During the ensuing naupliar and early copepodite phases, the larvae undergo substantial somatic growth, with metamorphosis—the transition from the final naupliar instar to the first copepodite stage—occurring after approximately 7.75 days  following hatching at the same temperature of 22 °C [T = 22 °C]. This relatively brief larval-juvenile stage is typical for small-bodied harpacticoids adapted to productive estuarine environments where food resources are abundant. The onset of first exogenous feeding in the nauplius begins shortly after hatching, as the yolk reserves are progressively depleted and the animal begins to graze on phytoplankton, a trophic switch that fuels the accelerated growth characteristic of this life stage.

As the juvenile copepodites continue their development, they undergo a series of molts that gradually increase body size toward the pubertal threshold. The isometric length at metamorphosis, measured when the individual completes its transition to the first copepodite instar, is 0.0150 centimeters . This measurement reflects the size at which the animal has achieved a critical developmental milestone, having passed through multiple naupliar stages characterized by rapid growth. The progression from the onset of exogenous feeding through the accelerating copepodite stage is marked by substantial linear increases in body length, culminating in the attainment of reproductive maturity. After metamorphosis, the copepodite stages continue to grow, with the isometric length at puberty, which is equivalent to the ultimate isometric length, recorded as 0.0283 centimeters [Lp = 0.0283 centimeters] for this species. This same value of 0.0283 centimeters [Li = 0.0283 centimeters] also represents the ultimate isometric length, the asymptotic size that characterizes fully mature individuals, a measurement consistent with the size at which growth ceases in this species. The time from metamorphosis to the onset of sexual maturation was observed to be 9.00 days [tp = 9.00 days] at 22 °C [T = 22 °C], after which the females develop functional gonads and become capable of producing their first egg clutch.

Reproductive output in Nitokra spinipes has been quantified through detailed observations of ovigerous females maintained in the laboratory. At 22 °C [T = 22 °C], females produce clutches containing a mean of 24 eggs per brood [N_R_i = 24 eggs per brood], and the inter-brood interval averages 3.17 days, yielding a frequency of approximately 115 broods per year [F_R_i = approximately 115 broods per year]. This high reproductive rate is characteristic of harpacticoid copepods that exploit ephemeral resources in dynamic brackish habitats. The ultimate dry weight of adult females, predicted from a linear regression of dry weight against total body length for harpacticoids, is 3.23 micrograms , a modest mass that facilitates rapid population turnover. Gravid females carry their embryonated eggs in attached egg sacs until the nauplii hatch, ensuring high offspring survival in the variable salinity conditions of estuarine sediments. The combination of relatively large brood sizes and short inter-brood intervals allows this species to achieve remarkable population densities under favorable conditions, a life-history strategy well-suited to its unpredictable coastal environment.

Metabolic demands in Nitokra spinipes have been evaluated through respirometry trials conducted on adults at their ultimate body size. At a reference temperature of 20 °C [T = 20 °C], the ultimate specific oxygen consumption of mature individuals averages 10.32 nanoliters per hour per microgram [JOi = 10.32 nanoliters per hour per microgram], a value derived from measurements on four brackish-water harpacticoid species. This mass-specific metabolic rate reflects the energetic costs associated with sustaining resting metabolic demands in a small-bodied ectotherm inhabiting thermally variable estuarine waters. Comparative data from related harpacticoid genera suggest that this level of oxygen consumption is consistent with the energetic requirements of active benthic foragers that continuously process sediment detritus and microalgae. The relatively low metabolic rate per unit mass, when considered alongside the species' high reproductive output, indicates that resources are directed toward offspring production rather than toward elevated maintenance costs. Such physiological traits are common among opportunistic colonizers of disturbed or ephemeral habitats where rapid population growth confers a selective advantage over less fecund competitors.

The complete life span of Nitokra spinipes, from egg fertilisation through natural mortality, has been estimated from laboratory cohorts maintained at 22 °C [T = 22 °C], with the maximum longevity recorded at approximately 108.9 days [am = approximately 108.9 days]. This relatively short life span is typical of small harpacticoid copepods, which exhibit rapid generation times and high population turnover rates in response to fluctuating environmental conditions. The brief age at hatch of 3.17 days  places N at a temperature of 22 °C [T = 22 °C]. spinipes among the faster-developing harpacticoids, likely reflecting an adaptation to unpredictable estuarine conditions where rapid early growth enhances survival. The rapid progression through larval and copepodite stages, and the early onset of reproduction, contribute to a life cycle that can be completed within a few weeks under optimal thermal regimes. The extended period of post-reproductive senescence, during which individuals may continue to feed and move but experience declining fecundity, represents a relatively small fraction of the total life span. Such a life-history configuration, characterized by early maturity, high fecundity, and short generation time, positions Nitokra spinipes as a classic r-selected species capable of rapid colonization of newly available habitats in the dynamic brackish-water ecosystems it inhabits.
